title: Image Generation
readingMarkdown:
# Image Generation

Type a sentence, get a picture. Image generation is the most immediately impressive thing ChatGPT does, and since 2025 it has also become one of the most practical: it can render readable text, follow long detailed instructions, and revise a picture across several turns of conversation. It is also easy to use badly. This chapter explains how it works, how to write an image prompt that gets what you intended, how to edit without the picture drifting, and what you may and may not do with the results.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### An illustrator who works from a written brief

Imagine commissioning an illustrator you can only reach by letter. You cannot point or sketch. Everything you want must be in the words, and anything you leave out, the illustrator will decide for you.

Write "a cat" and you will receive a cat: some cat, in some pose, in some style, somewhere. The illustrator did nothing wrong. Write "a ginger cat asleep on a windowsill in morning light, watercolour, soft pastel colours, seen from inside the room" and you receive something close to what was in your head.

Two properties of this illustrator explain most of what follows.

1. **Unspecified details are invented.** The model must fill every pixel. Whatever you did not describe is chosen for you, plausibly and arbitrarily.
2. **Each revision is a fresh drawing.** When you ask for a change, the illustrator does not erase one corner. They redraw the picture with your change in mind. Things you did not mention may shift.

### How it works, and why it changed

For years, image generators were **diffusion models**, covered in Module 1.5: they start from random noise and remove it step by step, guided by the text. ChatGPT's first image feature, in late 2023, worked this way. ChatGPT wrote a prompt and passed it to a separate image model, DALL-E 3.

In March 2025 OpenAI replaced that arrangement with image generation built into the main multimodal model. OpenAI described it as an **autoregressive** approach: the same model that reads your text and images also produces the image, piece by piece, as a continuation of the conversation.

```text
 OLD (2023):   you -> ChatGPT writes a prompt -> separate diffusion model -> image
                                 ^ the image model never saw your conversation

 NEW (2025+):  you -> one multimodal model reads text AND images -> image
                                 ^ sees the whole conversation, uploaded
                                   pictures, and its own earlier images
```

That architectural change is the reason for the practical improvements. Because one model handles everything, it can:

- use the full conversation as context, so "make it warmer" means something,
- look at images you upload and use them as references,
- render text far more accurately, since it understands the letters it is drawing,
- revise its own earlier image across several turns.

Later versions have added speed and, more recently, the ability to reason and to search the web before drawing. Model names in this area change every few months. The principles in this chapter have held across all of them.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### What it is good at, and where it fails

| Good at | Weak at |
|---|---|
| Following long, detailed descriptions | Scenes with many distinct objects, each with its own attributes |
| Readable text in common scripts | Small or dense text, and text in non-Latin scripts |
| Consistent style within one conversation | Keeping a character identical across many separate images |
| Editing by conversation | Changing one small region while leaving the rest pixel-identical |
| Diagrams and infographics that look right | Diagrams whose numbers and labels are actually correct |
| Using an uploaded image as a reference | Exact reproduction of a logo or a face |

OpenAI listed several of these limits itself when the feature launched: very tall or wide images can be cropped, details can be invented, the model struggles to bind attributes correctly once a scene has more than roughly ten to twenty objects, and precise edits can affect other parts of the picture.

The last row of the "weak at" column deserves emphasis because it looks like a strength. A generated chart or infographic can be beautifully laid out and contain invented figures. An image is a picture of information. Check every number and label in it.

### The anatomy of an image prompt

A complete image prompt answers six questions. OpenAI's own prompting guide recommends labelled sections for anything complex.

| Part | Question | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Subject | What is the picture of? | "A sourdough loaf on a wooden board, one slice cut" |
| Composition | How is it framed? | "Top-down view, loaf slightly left of centre, empty space on the right for text" |
| Style | What medium and look? | "Natural product photograph, shallow depth of field" |
| Lighting | What light and mood? | "Soft morning window light from the left, warm tones" |
| Text | What exact wording, where, in what lettering? | "The words 'Fresh Daily' in the top right, bold sans-serif, dark brown" |
| Constraints | What must or must not appear? | "No people. No other text. Plain linen background." |

Three techniques matter most.

**State the intended use.** "A poster for a shop window" and "an icon for a phone app" imply different detail, contrast, and composition. Telling the model the purpose lets it make sensible choices about everything you did not specify.

**Put text in quotation marks and say where it goes.** Write the exact words inside quotes, name the position and the lettering style, and add "no other text". For unusual names, spell them out letter by letter. Short text renders more reliably than long.

**Describe, do not name.** "In the style of" a living artist may be declined, and is in any case imprecise. Describing the qualities you want, such as "flat colours, thick outlines, limited palette of three colours", works better and avoids the problem.

### Editing without drift

Because each revision is a fresh drawing, vague edit requests cause unrelated changes. The remedy is a two-part instruction.

```text
 WEAK:    "Make it better and change the background."

 STRONG:  "Change only: the background, to a plain pale blue.
           Keep unchanged: the loaf, its position, the lighting,
           the text 'Fresh Daily' and its placement."
```

Change one thing per turn, and restate what must be preserved each time. After several rounds of edits, small unwanted changes accumulate, which practitioners call **drift**. When a picture has drifted, go back to the last good version and continue from there instead of trying to repair it. If a region must stay truly identical, such as a logo, add it afterwards in ordinary design software.

**Reference images.** You can upload pictures and give each a role: "use image 1 for the product, image 2 for the colour palette". Numbering them and stating the role avoids the model blending them in ways you did not intend.

### The arithmetic of image sizes

**Aspect ratio** is the proportion of width to height, reduced to lowest terms. For an image $W$ pixels wide and $H$ pixels high, divide both by their greatest common divisor:

$$
\text{aspect ratio} = \frac{W}{\gcd(W, H)} : \frac{H}{\gcd(W, H)}
$$

For $1536 \times 1024$ the greatest common divisor is 512, giving $3 : 2$.

**Megapixels** measure total resolution:

$$
\text{MP} = \frac{W \times H}{10^{6}}
$$

so $1536 \times 1024$ is about 1.57 megapixels.

Common platform shapes:

| Use | Aspect ratio |
|---|---|
| Square post, profile picture | 1:1 |
| Portrait feed post | 4:5 |
| Story, reel, phone wallpaper | 9:16 |
| Video thumbnail, slide, landscape banner | 16:9 |
| Standard photo print | 3:2 |

**Print size.** Printers need many more pixels than screens. The standard for good-quality print is 300 dots per inch (DPI), so

$$
\text{pixels needed} = \text{inches} \times \text{DPI}
$$

An A4 poster measures about $8.27 \times 11.69$ inches, which at 300 DPI needs roughly $2480 \times 3508$ pixels, about 8.7 megapixels. A standard $1024 \times 1536$ image printed at A4 size would have only about 124 pixels per inch and would look soft. Run the formula backwards to see what a given image can print well: $1536 \times 1024$ pixels at 300 DPI is about $5.1 \times 3.4$ inches, a small photograph.

**Size rules.** Through the developer API, standard sizes at the time of writing are $1024 \times 1024$, $1536 \times 1024$, and $1024 \times 1536$. Recent model generations also accept custom sizes within documented rules: both edges must be multiples of 16, the long edge may be at most three times the short edge, and the total number of pixels must fall within a permitted range, for one generation between 655,360 and 8,294,400. The upper figure is exactly $3840 \times 2160$. These limits differ between models, so treat them as an example of the kind of rule to check.

**Cost.** In ChatGPT, images count against a plan allowance that is separate from text messages. Through the API they are priced per image, by quality level and size. As an illustration from one published price list, a square image cost under one cent at low quality and about thirteen cents at high quality, a ratio of roughly fifteen to one. The practical habit: explore at low quality, and spend on high quality only for the final version.

### Rights, provenance, and policy

**Who owns the image?** OpenAI's terms assign whatever rights exist in the output to you, and permit commercial use, subject to its usage policies. That does not settle whether copyright exists at all. In the United States, the Copyright Office concluded in a January 2025 report that material generated entirely by AI, without sufficient human creative contribution, is not protected by copyright, and that writing a prompt is not by itself enough. In practice this means a purely generated image may be free for others to copy. Substantial human editing and arrangement can change the position. Law differs between countries and is still developing, so for anything commercially important, take advice.

**Provenance.** Images generated in ChatGPT carry **C2PA** metadata, an industry standard that records where an image came from. It lets platforms and tools identify the image as AI-generated. The metadata can be stripped by screenshots or re-saving, so its absence proves nothing. Do not present a generated image as a photograph of a real event.

**Policy.** Requests involving real, identifiable people, minors, and imitation of living artists are restricted in various ways, and the rules have changed over time. Expect some requests to be declined, and do not attempt to work around a refusal.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

Writing image prompts by hand leads to forgotten parts. A small builder enforces the structure from Section 2.

```python
ORDER = ["subject", "composition", "style", "lighting", "text", "constraints"]

def build_image_prompt(parts):
    """Assemble a labelled image prompt. Text is quoted exactly; constraints are joined."""
    if not str(parts.get("subject") or "").strip():
        raise ValueError("an image prompt needs a subject")
    lines = []
    for key in ORDER:
        value = parts.get(key)
        if not value:
            continue
        if key == "text":
            lines.append(f'Text (exact wording): "{value}". No other text.')
        elif key == "constraints":
            lines.append("Constraints: " + "; ".join(value))
        else:
            lines.append(f"{key.capitalize()}: {str(value).strip()}")
    return "\n".join(lines)

brief = {
    "subject": "A sourdough loaf on a wooden board, one slice cut",
    "composition": "Top-down view, loaf left of centre, empty space on the right",
    "style": "Natural product photograph, shallow depth of field",
    "lighting": "Soft morning window light from the left, warm tones",
    "text": "Fresh Daily",
    "constraints": ["no people", "plain linen background"],
}
print(build_image_prompt(brief))
```

- **A fixed order.** Subject first, constraints last. As with text prompts in Module 2.5, a consistent structure makes two versions easy to compare and makes a missing part obvious.
- **The text line does three jobs.** It puts the wording in quotation marks, labels it as exact, and adds "No other text". Each addresses a known failure: paraphrased wording, misspelling, and stray lettering.
- **Constraints are a list.** Separate items are easier to check against the result than a sentence.
- **A missing subject is an error.** Everything else is optional, because the model will choose sensibly. Without a subject there is nothing to draw.

Next, the size arithmetic.

```python
import math

def aspect_ratio(width, height):
    divisor = math.gcd(width, height)
    return f"{width // divisor}:{height // divisor}"

def megapixels(width, height):
    return width * height / 1_000_000

def size_problems(width, height, min_pixels=655_360, max_pixels=8_294_400):
    """Check a custom size against one model generation's documented rules."""
    problems = []
    if width % 16 or height % 16:
        problems.append("not_multiple_of_16")
    if max(width, height) > 3 * min(width, height):
        problems.append("ratio_too_extreme")
    if width * height > max_pixels:
        problems.append("too_many_pixels")
    if width * height < min_pixels:
        problems.append("too_few_pixels")
    return sorted(problems)

for w, h in ((1536, 1024), (1920, 1080), (3840, 2160), (4000, 1000), (1000, 1000)):
    print(f"{w}x{h}: {aspect_ratio(w, h):>5}  {megapixels(w, h):5.2f} MP  {size_problems(w, h) or 'ok'}")

print(f"A4 at 300 DPI: {round(8.27 * 300)} x {round(11.69 * 300)} pixels")
print(f"1536x1024 prints at {1536 / 300:.1f} x {1024 / 300:.1f} inches at 300 DPI")
```

- **`math.gcd` does the reduction.** Dividing both edges by their greatest common divisor gives the ratio in lowest terms: 1920 by 1080 becomes 16:9.
- **`width % 16` is zero when the width is a multiple of 16.** In Python, zero counts as false, so `if width % 16 or height % 16` reads as "if either edge leaves a remainder".
- **The ratio rule compares the long edge with three times the short edge.** Writing it with `max` and `min` handles portrait and landscape with one line.
- **The table shows three different failures.** 1920 by 1080 is a perfectly ordinary screen size and fails, because 1080 is not a multiple of 16. The nearest valid size is 1920 by 1088. 4000 by 1000 fails on shape, and on the multiple rule as well. 1000 by 1000 fails on the multiple rule alone. Discovering this in code is quicker than discovering it from a rejected request.
- **The print lines apply the DPI formula in both directions.** A4 needs about 2481 by 3507 pixels, and a standard landscape image prints well only at about 5 by 3.4 inches.

Finally, edit instructions and cost.

```python
def edit_instruction(change, keep):
    """A precise edit: one change, and an explicit list of what must not change."""
    if keep:
        return f"Change only: {change}. Keep unchanged: {', '.join(keep)}."
    return f"Change only: {change}. Keep everything else unchanged."

EXAMPLE_PRICES = {"low": (0.009, 0.013), "medium": (0.034, 0.05), "high": (0.133, 0.20)}   # (square, other)

def image_cost(count, quality, square=True, prices=EXAMPLE_PRICES):
    return count * prices[quality][0 if square else 1]

print(edit_instruction("the background, to plain pale blue", ["the loaf", "the lighting", "the text 'Fresh Daily'"]))
print(f"20 drafts at low quality:  USD {image_cost(20, 'low'):.2f}")
print(f"20 drafts at high quality: USD {image_cost(20, 'high'):.2f}")
```

The edit helper encodes the rule from Section 2 so it cannot be forgotten: every edit names one change and states what is preserved. The cost lines make the exploration habit concrete. Twenty drafts cost eighteen cents at low quality and USD 2.66 at high quality, for pictures you will mostly discard. The prices are examples from one model's published list and will have changed. The ratio between quality levels is the durable point.

**Complexity.** All of these are constant-time calculations. The Euclidean algorithm behind `math.gcd` takes a number of steps proportional to the number of digits in the inputs.

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**Text is better than it was, and still needs proofreading.** Short headlines usually render correctly. Long sentences, small print, and unusual names are where letters go wrong. Read every word in the image before using it, and for anything important add the text afterwards in a design tool.

**Check the numbers in any chart or infographic.** A generated diagram is a drawing of a diagram. Its figures, labels, and even its arithmetic may be invented. Supply the real data in the prompt and verify the result against it.

**Drift is real. Go back; do not patch.** After several edits, faces, colours, and layouts shift in small ways. Experienced users keep the last good version and branch from it, and they restate what must be preserved in every edit request.

**One change per turn.** Asking for three changes at once makes it hard to tell which one caused an unwanted side effect, the same lesson as prompt debugging in Module 2.5.

**Your prompt may be rewritten.** The application can expand or adjust your request before the image is produced. If results ignore a specific instruction, state it more plainly, put it earlier, and say that it is a requirement.

**Consistent characters across separate images are hard.** Within one conversation, consistency is reasonable. Across many images for a series, expect variation. Upload a reference image each time, describe fixed features explicitly, and generate the set in one conversation where possible.

**Get the shape right first.** An image generated square cannot be turned into a good 9:16 story by cropping without losing the subject. State the aspect ratio or the intended platform at the start.

**Generated images are low resolution for print.** A standard output is fine for a screen and soft on a poster. Check the pixel dimensions against the print size before promising a client a printed product, and plan for upscaling or a different tool.

**Limits are separate from text limits and are not published as a stable table.** People are surprised to hit an image cap while having text messages left. The application shows when the allowance resets.

**Do not assume you own it exclusively.** Purely generated images may have no copyright protection in some countries, which means a competitor could reuse them. For logos and brand assets, where exclusivity matters, involve a human designer and take legal advice.

**Real people and brands are a risk.** Likenesses, trademarks, and recognisable characters can create legal problems regardless of what the tool allows. A refusal is information, and so is a result that looks too much like someone else's property.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** Image generation in ChatGPT moved in 2025 from a separate diffusion model fed by a written prompt to generation inside the main multimodal model, which is why it can now use the whole conversation, read uploaded images, render text, and revise its own work. It behaves like an illustrator working from a written brief: unspecified details are invented, and every revision is a fresh drawing. A complete prompt states subject, composition, style, lighting, exact text, and constraints, along with the intended use. Edits should change one thing and name what must stay the same. Aspect ratio comes from dividing width and height by their greatest common divisor, resolution is width times height, and print needs about 300 pixels per inch. Explore cheaply and finalise at high quality. Generated images carry provenance metadata, may not be protected by copyright, and must always be proofread for text and checked for invented facts.

**Question 1.** A user asks for "a poster for my bakery" and receives a square image with the shop name misspelled and a person in the background they did not want. Using the six parts of an image prompt, explain each failure and write a better request.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The request specified only a vague subject. No composition or shape was given, so the model chose square. No text was specified exactly, so the model invented or approximated the lettering. No constraints were given, so the model filled the scene with whatever seemed plausible, including a person. A better request: "Subject: a sourdough loaf and two croissants on a wooden counter. Composition: portrait poster, 2:3, products in the lower half, clear space in the upper third for the title. Style: warm natural product photograph. Lighting: soft morning light from the left. Text (exact wording): 'Marigold Bakery' at the top, large serif lettering, dark brown; spell it M-A-R-I-G-O-L-D. No other text. Constraints: no people, no hands, plain background. Intended use: a printed shop-window poster." Each addition removes a decision the model would otherwise make arbitrarily.

</details>

**Question 2.** An image is 1920 by 1080 pixels. Compute its aspect ratio and megapixels, and work out the largest size at which it can be printed at 300 DPI. Is it suitable for an A4 poster?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The greatest common divisor of 1920 and 1080 is 120, so the aspect ratio is 16:9. The resolution is 1920 times 1080, which is 2,073,600 pixels, about 2.07 megapixels. At 300 DPI it prints at 1920 divided by 300 by 1080 divided by 300 inches, which is 6.4 by 3.6 inches. An A4 sheet is about 8.27 by 11.69 inches and needs roughly 2480 by 3508 pixels at 300 DPI, about 8.7 megapixels. The image has less than a quarter of the pixels required and is also the wrong shape, landscape 16:9 against A4 portrait. It is not suitable. It would need to be regenerated in a portrait shape at a much higher resolution, or upscaled with a dedicated tool, accepting some loss of sharpness.

</details>

**Question 3.** After five rounds of edits, the product in an image has subtly changed colour and the lettering has shifted position, though the user never asked for either. Explain why this happens and describe the working method that prevents it.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Each edit produces a newly generated image conditioned on the previous one and the instruction. It is not a local change to stored pixels. Details that the instruction did not mention are free to vary a little each time, and over several rounds those small variations accumulate into visible drift. The preventive method has four parts. Make one change per turn, so side effects can be traced. Write each edit as "change only X; keep unchanged A, B, C", restating the elements that must be preserved every time. Keep the last version you were satisfied with and, when drift appears, return to it and branch from there instead of trying to correct the drifted image. And for elements that must be truly identical, such as a logo or exact lettering, add them afterwards in design software.

</details>

steps.instruction: Implement build_image_prompt(parts). Raise ValueError with the message an image prompt needs a subject if the subject is missing or blank. Otherwise go through ORDER and add one line for each key with a non-empty value. For 'text', the line is Text (exact wording): followed by the value in double quotes, a full stop, and the sentence No other text. For any other key, the line is the key with a capital first letter, a colon, and the stripped value. Join the lines with newlines. [MOD-2.9]
steps.hintConceptual: An image prompt is a brief with six parts. Anything you omit is decided for you, so the builder's job is to make sure the parts you care about are stated, in a fixed order, with the text spelled out exactly.

steps.title: Aspect ratio and megapixels
steps.instruction: Implement aspect_ratio(width, height). Find the greatest common divisor of the two numbers with math.gcd, divide both by it using integer division, and return a string of the two results separated by a colon. Then implement megapixels(width, height) as width times height divided by one million. These are the two formulas from Section 2 that tell you an image's shape and its total resolution. [MOD-2.9]
steps.hintConceptual: The shape of an image is its width and height with every common factor removed. Its resolution is simply how many pixels it contains in total.
steps.hintSyntax:
# aspect_ratio
divisor = math.gcd(width, height)
return f"{width // divisor}:{height // divisor}"

# megapixels
return width * height / 1_000_000

Return a sorted list of violations: 'not_multiple_of_16' if either edge is not divisible by 16, 'ratio_too_extreme' if the longer edge is more than three times the shorter, 'too_many_pixels' if the total exceeds max_pixels, and 'too_few_pixels' if it is below min_pixels. An empty list means the size is acceptable. Try 1920 by 1080, a very common screen size, and see why it is rejected. [MOD-2.9]
steps.hintConceptual: Image models accept only certain shapes and sizes. Checking the rules yourself, before sending a request, tells you exactly which rule a size breaks and what the nearest valid size would be.
steps.testAssertion:
assert size_problems(1536, 1024) == [], "1536x1024 is a valid size"
assert size_problems(1920, 1080) == ["not_multiple_of_16"], "1080 is not a multiple of 16"
assert size_problems(1920, 1088) == [], "1920x1088 is the nearest valid size to full HD"
assert size_problems(3840, 2160) == [], "3840x2160 is exactly at the pixel limit and is allowed"
assert size_problems(4000, 1000) == ["not_multiple_of_16", "ratio_too_extreme"], "4000x1000 breaks two rules (1000 is not a multiple of 16, and 4:1 is too wide)"
assert size_problems(1024, 3072) == [], "A ratio of exactly 3:1 is allowed, in portrait too"
assert size_problems(1024, 3088) == ["ratio_too_extreme"], "Slightly beyond 3:1 is rejected"
assert size_problems(4096, 4096) == ["too_many_pixels"], "4096x4096 has too many pixels"
assert size_problems(512, 512) == ["too_few_pixels"], "512x512 has too few pixels"
assert size_problems(512, 512, min_pixels=1000) == [], "The min_pixels argument must be respected"
print("Step 3 passed: full HD (1920x1080) is rejected; 1920x1088 is accepted.")

steps.title: Screen pixels and print inches
steps.instruction: Implement print_inches(width, height, dpi), which returns a tuple of the width and height in inches when printed at the given dots per inch: each pixel dimension divided by dpi. Then implement pixels_for_print(width_inches, height_inches, dpi), which returns a tuple of the pixel dimensions needed, each rounded to the nearest whole number. These apply the formula pixels = inches times DPI from Section 2 in both directions, and show why a standard generated image is too small for a poster. [MOD-2.9]
steps.hintConceptual: A printer lays down a fixed number of dots per inch, usually 300 for good quality. Dividing pixels by that number gives the print size; multiplying inches by it gives the pixels you need.
steps.hintSyntax:
# print_inches
return width / dpi, height / dpi

# pixels_for_print
return round(width_inches * dpi), round(height_inches * dpi)
steps.testAssertion:
assert print_inches(1536, 1024) == (5.12, 1024 / 300), f"1536x1024 at 300 DPI is 5.12 by about 3.41 inches, got {print_inches(1536, 1024)}"
assert print_inches(3000, 2400) == (10.0, 8.0), "3000x2400 at 300 DPI is 10 by 8 inches"
assert print_inches(1920, 1080, dpi=96) == (20.0, 11.25), "The dpi argument must be respected"
assert pixels_for_print(8.27, 11.69) == (2481, 3507), f"A4 at 300 DPI needs 2481 by 3507 pixels, got {pixels_for_print(8.27, 11.69)}"
assert pixels_for_print(10, 8) == (3000, 2400), "A 10 by 8 inch print needs 3000 by 2400 pixels"
assert pixels_for_print(4, 6, dpi=150) == (600, 900), "At 150 DPI a 4 by 6 inch print needs 600 by 900 pixels"
_w, _h = pixels_for_print(8.27, 11.69)
assert _w * _h > 5 * 1536 * 1024, "An A4 poster needs more than five times the pixels of a standard 1536x1024 image"
print("Step 4 passed: a standard image prints well at about 5 by 3.4 inches, not at poster size.")

steps.title: Precise edits and cost
steps.instruction: Implement edit_instruction(change, keep). If keep is a non-empty list, return the sentence Change only: followed by the change and a full stop, then Keep unchanged: followed by the items joined with a comma and a space, and a full stop. If keep is empty, the second sentence is Keep everything else unchanged. Then implement image_cost(count, quality, square, prices): look up the quality in prices, take the first number for a square image and the second otherwise, and multiply by count. One change per edit and cheap drafts are the two working habits from Section 2. [MOD-2.9]
steps.hintConceptual: Every revision redraws the whole picture, so an edit must name what changes and what stays. And since most drafts are thrown away, they should be generated at the cheapest quality.
steps.hintSyntax:
# edit_instruction
if keep:
    return f"Change only: {change}. Keep unchanged: {', '.join(keep)}."
return f"Change only: {change}. Keep everything else unchanged."

# image_cost
return count * prices[quality][0 if square else 1]
steps.testAssertion:
assert edit_instruction("the background to pale blue", ["the loaf", "the lighting"]) == "Change only: the background to pale blue. Keep unchanged: the loaf, the lighting.", f"Unexpected instruction: {edit_instruction('the background to pale blue', ['the loaf', 'the lighting'])!r}"
assert edit_instruction("the title to 'Open Now'", []) == "Change only: the title to 'Open Now'. Keep everything else unchanged.", "With nothing listed, everything else is to be kept"
assert edit_instruction("the sky", ["the house"]) == "Change only: the sky. Keep unchanged: the house.", "A single item is listed without a trailing comma"
assert abs(image_cost(20, "low") - 0.18) < 1e-9, "20 square low-quality images cost USD 0.18"
assert abs(image_cost(20, "high") - 2.66) < 1e-9, "20 square high-quality images cost USD 2.66"
assert abs(image_cost(4, "medium", square=False) - 0.20) < 1e-9, "4 non-square medium images cost USD 0.20"
assert image_cost(0, "high") == 0, "No images cost nothing"
assert abs(image_cost(3, "draft", prices={"draft": (0.5, 1.0)}) - 1.5) < 1e-9, "The prices argument must be used"
print("Step 5 passed: twenty drafts cost USD 0.18 at low quality and USD 2.66 at high.")
